(WIRED) -- Two cable powerhouses have announced an ambitious pilot program that aims to convince their customers that, actually, TV on the web should not be free. Jeffrey Bewkes, chairman and CEO of Time Warner, speaks at the NCTA conference in Washington. With a service called TV Everywhere, Comcast and Time Warner will give cable subscribers access to "premium" television content via broadband, and later cellphone connections. To begin with, 5,000 Comcast subscribers will begin testing the system next month, giving them access to Time Warner's TBS and TNT channels on their computers, and the same channels' video-on-demand catalogs on their cable boxes. If you made peace long ago with the idea of paying a monthly cable bill, this probably sounds great. It means watching your existing subscription on new screens without paying additional fees or buying more hardware. (Of course, as consumers adopt TV Everywhere, they can probably expect price increases.) But if you prefer to watch your television for free on ad-supported sites like Hulu while paying only for the internet connection that delivers it, you could be in for a rude awakening. TV Everywhere represents an alternative -- and possible threat -- to the popular Hulu model. If the pilot program impresses the group -- and proves to other networks that its user-authentication system is secure -- Comcast and Time Warner expect the other television programmers, ISPs and mobile providers to join, giving all cable subscribers a way to watch the content they pay for on their televisions using any broadband-connected computer or authenticated cellphone. Already "at least 92 percent of Americans qualify to watch this for free online," according to Jeff Bewkes, chairman and CEO of Time Warner. For these subscribers, TV Everywhere represents a potential win. The only question is whether they will keep paying for the old cable subscription model as their viewing habits shift online. There's nothing to stop television networks from putting their content on both Hulu and TV Everywhere, because TV Everywhere's contract will be non-exclusive, according to Bewkes. However, given the choice between Hulu and TV Everywhere, television programmers have an incentive to go with the latter. Only the TV Everywhere model promises to port yesterday's lucrative business model onto today's platforms. And that, according to some critics, is exactly the problem. "[TV Everywhere] raises substantial anti-competitive issues by restricting the availability of programming to the favored distribution methods," said Gigi B. Sohn, president and co-founder of the public interest group Public Knowledge. "Under the TV Everywhere plan, no other program distributors would be able to emerge, and no consumers will be able to 'cut the cord' because they find what they want online. As a result, consumers will be the losers. "In addition, we are concerned that this program violates the open nature of the internet. By adding this additional toll lane, Comcast and Time Warner want to create their own 'managed channel' within the internet and turn the internet into their own private cable channel." So, what about Hulu? Will its deals fall through given this new option? "There will be some part [of Time Warner's content] that will be out there [on Hulu], said Bewkes."Short-form content, I think, will continue to be available -- promotional content will continue to be available." However, only cable subscribers will be able to access other content online -- through officially licensed avenues, anyway. Bewkes added that some other television programmers have avoided Hulu "for security concerns and because they didn't like the model," but that they will give TV Everywhere a chance. "Consumers vote every single month with their pocketbook," he added. "They don't have to subscribe to cable. They don't have to pay for these services, yet they do. The number of people paying for subscription television has gone up and up and up every single quarter that we've been in the business." ***

**(WIRED)** — Two cable industry powerhouses have announced an ambitious pilot program designed to persuade consumers that premium online television content should carry a price tag. Speaking at the NCTA conference in Washington, D.C., Jeffrey Bewkes, Chairman and CEO of Time Warner, outlined the strategy behind the initiative.

Dubbed **"TV Everywhere,"** the joint venture between Comcast and Time Warner will grant cable subscribers access to premium television content via broadband networks, with mobile integration planned for a later phase. The trial launches next month with an initial testing group of 5,000 Comcast subscribers, who will receive online access to Time Warner’s TBS and TNT networks, as well as video-on-demand catalogs for those channels directly through their set-top boxes.

For existing cable subscribers, this initiative offers a compelling benefit: the ability to stream subscribed content across multiple devices without purchasing additional hardware or incurring immediate extra fees (though long-term price increases remain a distinct possibility as adoption grows). Conversely, for consumers accustomed to viewing television for free on ad-supported platforms like Hulu while paying solely for an internet connection, this shift signals a potential disruption to the status quo. 

TV Everywhere poses a direct alternative—and a potential challenge—to the ad-supported model popularized by Hulu. Should the pilot succeed in proving the security of its user-authentication system, Comcast and Time Warner anticipate that other networks, internet service providers (ISPs), and mobile carriers will follow suit. This would allow cable subscribers nationwide to access paid television content across any broadband-connected computer or authenticated mobile device.

According to Bewkes, "at least 92 percent of Americans currently qualify" to access this content online at no extra charge. For this demographic, TV Everywhere represents a clear value addition. The critical question, however, is whether consumers will maintain traditional cable subscriptions as viewing habits increasingly shift online. 

While networks remain free to distribute content on both Hulu and TV Everywhere—given the non-exclusive nature of TV Everywhere’s contracts—content creators have a strong incentive to favor the cable-backed model. TV Everywhere stands alone in its ability to translate the television industry’s traditionally lucrative business model onto modern digital platforms.

Yet, this very structure is precisely what draws criticism. "[TV Everywhere] raises substantial anti-competitive issues by restricting the availability of programming to the favored distribution methods," stated Gigi B. Sohn, President and Co-founder of the public interest group Public Knowledge. "Under the TV Everywhere plan, no other program distributors would be able to emerge, and no consumers will be able to 'cut the cord' because they find what they want online. As a result, consumers will be the losers."

Sohn added, "In addition, we are concerned that this program violates the open nature of the internet. By adding this additional toll lane, Comcast and Time Warner want to create their own 'managed channel' within the internet and turn the internet into their own private cable channel."

This strategy raises questions regarding the future of third-party streaming services: will content deals on platforms like Hulu falter under this new framework? 

"There will be some part [of Time Warner's content] that will be out there [on Hulu]," Bewkes noted. "Short-form content, I think, will continue to be available—promotional content will continue to be available." 

However, full-length content via officially licensed online channels will be restricted strictly to authenticated cable subscribers. Bewkes added that several television programmers previously avoided Hulu due to "security concerns and because they didn't like the model," but are eager to adopt TV Everywhere.

"Consumers vote every single month with their pocketbook," Bewkes concluded. "They don't have to subscribe to cable. They don't have to pay for these services, yet they do. The number of people paying for subscription television has gone up and up and up every single quarter that we've been in the business."

In response to rapidly changing media consumption habits, cable giants Comcast and Time Warner have joined forces to launch a groundbreaking pilot program dubbed "TV Everywhere." This collaborative initiative is designed to allow traditional cable subscribers to stream premium television content directly on their computers, smartphones, and mobile devices, effectively expanding the boundaries of traditional television viewing.

A key feature of the TV Everywhere service is its seamless integration into existing customer packages. Current subscribers can access their paid channels on these new digital screens without requiring immediate extra fees or the purchase of new hardware. By utilizing a simple authentication process, the service provides added value to current customers, giving them the flexibility to watch their favorite programming anytime and anywhere.

Strategically, this model represents a major effort to defend the traditional entertainment ecosystem. By tying digital content access strictly to a paid cable subscription, TV Everywhere establishes a direct alternative—and a significant competitive threat—to free, ad-supported streaming platforms such as Hulu. Rather than allowing digital audiences to migrate away to free online alternatives, the cable providers are creating a gated experience that reinforces the value of a monthly cable package.

The current launch serves as a testing ground for a much broader industry shift. If the initial trial proves both commercially successful and technologically secure against digital piracy, Comcast and Time Warner plan to aggressively expand the service. The long-term vision involves onboarding additional television programmers, internet service providers, and mobile networks to build an industry-wide standard.

**Title:** The Digital Pivot: How "TV Everywhere" Redefined the Cable Landscape

As consumer habits rapidly evolve, the living room couch is no longer the sole destination for television consumption. Millions of viewers are shifting their viewing habits toward web browsers, smartphones, and mobile devices, demanding access to their favorite shows anytime and anywhere. In response to this seismic shift, legacy media titans Comcast and Time Warner have launched an ambitious initiative known as "TV Everywhere." Designed as a bridge between traditional cable infrastructure and the digital frontier, this strategic framework aims to modernize television distribution without undermining the lucrative cable subscription model.

At the heart of the "TV Everywhere" initiative is a secure user-authentication system. Rather than launching an entirely new, standalone streaming service, cable operators are integrating digital access directly into existing home subscriptions. Under this model, subscribers simply log into online portals or mobile applications using their cable account credentials. Once authenticated, users gain high-definition, multi-screen access to live broadcasts and on-demand premium content from networks like HBO, TNT, and TBS—at no additional cost beyond their standard monthly bill.

Crucial to the initiative's immediate potential is its unprecedented scale. Because over 92 percent of American households already subscribe to a traditional pay-TV service, the vast majority of consumers automatically qualify for "TV Everywhere" access from day one. This massive installed base gives cable providers an enormous competitive advantage. Rather than spending millions of dollars trying to acquire new digital-only subscribers from scratch, Comcast and Time Warner are using multi-screen flexibility to add value to existing packages, thereby reducing subscriber churn and disincentivizing "cord-cutting."

Beyond retaining current customers, "TV Everywhere" poses a direct and formidable strategic threat to free, ad-supported streaming platforms such as Hulu. In the early days of online video, platforms like Hulu thrived by offering full, recent episodes of popular network shows for free, monetized only by short digital ad breaks. However, by establishing a secure system that locks premium content behind a subscription wall, cable giants and content creators can restrict the flow of top-tier programming to open web platforms. 

As media conglomerates increasingly prioritize authenticated access, free platforms face the grim prospect of losing rights to current-season hits, exclusive sports broadcasts, and high-budget original series. Advertisers, too, may follow the premium content to authenticated channels, where higher user engagement and verified demographic data command better ad rates.

Ultimately, the rollout of "TV Everywhere" by Comcast and Time Warner represents a pivotal moment in media history. By leveraging their existing market dominance and implementing robust authentication technology, cable companies are proving that traditional pay-TV can adapt to the digital age. In doing so, they are not only reshaping how consumers access entertainment across multiple screens, but also redrawing the battle lines of the online streaming economy.

The glow of the neon headline illuminated the glass desk where the latest issue of *WIRED* lay open. On the cover, bathed in stark, minimalist lighting, was Jeffrey—a man who had spent the last decade working in complete digital solitude, far from the glare of Silicon Valley.

To the outside world, Jeffrey was a ghost. To the tech elite who devoured the pages of *WIRED*, he was the elusive architect of the next digital frontier. The article’s title was simple, printed in bold sans-serif across his chest: *The Duality of Man and Machine.*

Inside the profile, the story unpacked Jeffrey’s quiet revolution. He hadn't built another bloated social network or a flash-in-the-pan crypto protocol. Instead, Jeffrey had spent ten years developing an artificial intelligence model known simply as "Two." 

The name wasn't just a placeholder for a second iteration; it was a philosophy. While the rest of the tech industry scrambled to build monolithic systems with billions of chaotic parameters, Jeffrey believed true synthetic intelligence required a partner. "Two" was a bi-nodal neural network—two distinct digital minds locked in a permanent, hyper-fast dialogue with one another. One half of Two was programmed for hyper-logic and deduction; the other was driven by predictive, almost intuitive pattern recognition. They debated, corrected, and balanced each other in milliseconds.

"One mind creates a monologue," Jeffrey was quoted in the *WIRED* piece, his gaze steady in the accompanying portrait. "Three becomes a chorus of noise. But two... two is a conversation."

The journalist who wrote the profile recalled visiting Jeffrey’s remote laboratory in the Pacific Northwest. There were no foosball tables or artisanal coffee bars—just racks of silent, liquid-cooled servers humming in the damp woods. Through *WIRED*, the world finally got a glimpse of what Jeffrey and Two had accomplished: a system capable of predicting complex climate shifts and decoding protein structures at twice the speed of any supercomputer on Earth, all through the art of digital debate.

As night fell, Jeffrey closed the digital preview of the article on his monitor. He looked over at the dual terminal screens glowing quietly in his lab. On the left screen, Node A blinked. On the right, Node B responded. 

He smiled, picked up the print issue of *WIRED*, and placed it on the shelf. The world was finally listening to the conversation, but Jeffrey knew that he and Two were only just getting started.

**WIRED** | GEAR | TECH BIZ | ENTERTAINMENT

# Cable’s Empire Strikes Back: Comcast and Time Warner Launch ‘TV Everywhere’ to Kill the Free Web

**Afraid of a future dominated by Hulu and browser-bound cord-cutters, the pay-TV giants are walling off online video behind your monthly cable bill.**

**By Eliot Van Buskirk**  
*June 25, 2009 | 12:00 PM*

For the past two years, watching TV on the web felt like a glimpse into a utopian, post-cable future. You opened a web browser, navigated to Hulu or YouTube, clicked play, and watched *30 Rock* in crisp, high-definition Flash video—no set-top box, no long-term contract, and most importantly, not a single penny paid to a cable company. 

The cable industry’s response to this digital rebellion has finally arrived, and it goes by the deceptively consumer-friendly name “TV Everywhere.”

Announced in a joint push by Time Warner CEO Jeff Bewkes and Comcast chief Brian Roberts, TV Everywhere is the cable industry’s grand strategy to bring the lucrative pay-TV model to the internet. The concept is simple, albeit aggressively defensive: If you want to stream current-season cable and broadcast shows online, you have to prove you already pay for a traditional cable subscription. 

No cable bill? No video.

"Our goal is to give consumers access to the great content they already pay for, anytime and anywhere," Comcast's Roberts declared during a demonstration of the technology this week. But strip away the corporate gloss, and TV Everywhere looks less like a feature and more like a fortress. It is a digital moat designed to protect the cable industry's $60-billion-a-year subscription ecosystem from the existential threat of web-native streaming.

### The Hulu Problem

At the center of the cable giants’ panic is Hulu. The joint venture between NBC Universal, News Corp., and Disney has rapidly become the poster child for the free, ad-supported web video boom. Millions of young viewers—a demographic tech analysts are beginning to call "cord-cutters"—are realizing that a fast broadband connection and a laptop connected to an HDTV render a $100-a-month digital cable bundle obsolete.

TV Everywhere aims to nip that behavior in the bud. Under the new initiative, Comcast and Time Warner will launch online portals requiring users to sign in with their cable account credentials. Once authenticated, users get access to thousands of hours of prime-time shows, movies, and live sports. 

If it sounds like a clunky solution to a problem internet users had already solved, that's because it is. While Hulu requires zero authentication and loads instantly, TV Everywhere introduces a layer of digital rights management (DRM) friction. You aren't just a web surfer anymore; you are a verified subscriber entering a walled garden.

"TV Everywhere is an attempt to turn back the clock," says James McQuivey, a media analyst at Forrester Research. "Cable operators spent decades building a closed ecosystem, and Hulu blew the door off. TV Everywhere is their attempt to put the lock back on the door before the web destroys their broadcast margins."

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|  THE 2009 STREAMING LANDSCAPE: TWO CONFLICTING VISIONS      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|  HULU / THE FREE WEB        |  TV EVERYWHERE (CABLE)        |
|  • Free, ad-supported       |  • Tied to $80+ cable bill    |
|  • Frictionless browser access| • Mandatory user login/DRM  |
|  • Unbundled, on-demand     |  • Preserves the cable bundle |
|  • Target: Cord-cutters     |  • Target: Cable loyalists    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### A House Divided

The initiative creates a bizarre paradox for the media conglomerates powering it. Take NBC Universal, for instance. NBC is a major stakeholder in Hulu, benefiting from the site's massive traffic and sleek user interface. Yet NBC is also scrambling to sign deals with Comcast to put its content behind the TV Everywhere paywall. 

Networks are terrified of angering the cable operators who pay them millions in retransmission fees. If Comcast threatens to drop a network from its channel lineup, that network will fall in line—even if it means pulling popular shows off the free web and hiding them behind an authentication screen.

Rumors are already circulating in Silicon Valley that NBC, Fox, and ABC may soon start delaying when new episodes appear on Hulu, giving TV Everywhere subscribers a exclusive 30-day window. If that happens, the frictionless Hulu experience consumers have come to love could be crippled by design.

### Will Web Viewers Bite?

The ultimate question is whether tech-savvy consumers will accept the cable industry's terms. The internet has spent fifteen years training users that content wants to be free—or at least easy to access. 

Technologically, TV Everywhere feels like a relic of mid-2000s corporate compromise. Authenticating through a cable provider’s bloated portal to watch a Flash stream on a 13-inch MacBook screen is a far cry from the seamless elegance of modern web apps. Furthermore, as smartphones grow more capable and internet-connected TVs begin to hit store shelves, a browser-based authentication gate feels painfully short-sighted.

Comcast and Time Warner are banking on the idea that high-quality content will trump user convenience. They believe that if they lock up *Mad Men*, *The Office*, and live sports behind a paywall, viewers will have no choice but to keep paying their monthly cable bills.

They might be right in the short term. But by trying to force the open web into a 1990s pay-TV box, the cable industry isn't stopping the streaming revolution—it's just delaying it. For now, the war for the living room has moved to the browser window, and cable's dinosaurs have made it clear they won't go extinct without a fight.

***

*Eliot Van Buskirk covers tech and digital music for WIRED. Spotted a new streaming portal? Tell us in the comments below.*

# WALLING OFF THE WEB
### Comcast and Time Warner are betting $100 billion that you’ll log into your cable account to watch TV online. Will web surfers bite—or stick with Hulu?

**BY MIKE MONTGOMERY**  
**07.24.2009 | 12:00 PM**

---

If you spent the last year watching *30 Rock* on your MacBook while lounging in a coffee shop, the gods of traditional media have a message for you: The free lunch is almost over.

Determined to halt a growing trickle of web-savvy "cord-cutters" from ditching their set-top boxes in favor of sleek, zero-dollar web portals, the traditional cable industry is preparing its most ambitious counteroffensive yet. It’s called "TV Everywhere," and this month, the empire officially began striking back.

In a tightly controlled pilot program launched last week, cable giant Comcast and media titan Time Warner quietly rolled out online streaming access to 5,000 select Comcast subscribers. For the first time, these lucky test subjects can stream full-length, high-definition episodes from two of Time Warner’s flagship basic-cable networks—TBS and TNT—directly on their computer screens. 

There’s just one catch: You can’t just click play. 

Before you can watch Conan O'Brien riffs or *The Closer* reruns, you have to prove you’re already paying a fat monthly cable bill. Users must pass through a digital turnstile, authenticating their subscription by typing in their Comcast account details. If you're a cable subscriber, the web content is "free." If you’ve already cut the wire? You get a blank screen.

It is a stark, defensive contrast to Hulu—the joint venture between NBC Universal and News Corp. that has rapidly become the darling of digital video. Hulu’s siren song has always been pure, frictionless simplicity: Open a browser, endure a 15-second pre-roll ad, and watch prime-time television without paying a dime or showing an ID. 

To Time Warner CEO Jeff Bewkes, the architect behind the TV Everywhere concept, Hulu’s free-for-all model is not just unsustainable—it’s economic suicide. 

"Free web video is a fantasy that misunderstands how high-quality television actually gets funded," Bewkes told reporters during a recent industry briefing on the authentication strategy. "TV Everywhere isn't about restricting access; it’s about extending the enormous value of the cable package to every screen you own. If you already pay for TNT through your cable provider, you should have it on your laptop, your iPhone, anywhere. But the idea that premium programming should just be given away online for free without a subscription? That’s not a business model. That’s a charity."

Bewkes and Comcast head Brian Roberts hope the 5,000-user trial will prove that consumers are willing to jump through the authentication hoop if it means getting legitimate, authorized streams of their favorite shows. If successful, the initiative will expand rapidly to millions of homes, sucking dozens of other networks—from HBO to ESPN—into the authenticated "walled garden."

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         JARGON WATCH                            |
|                                                                 |
| Authentication (n.): The digital velvet rope requiring web     |
| users to log in with their cable ISP credentials before         |
| viewing premium video online. See also: "Paywall 2.0."          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Unsurprisingly, public interest groups and digital rights advocates are sounding the alarm, arguing that TV Everywhere is less about convenient multi-screen access and more about preserving a cozy, legacy oligopoly.

Gigi B. Sohn, president and co-founder of the public interest group Public Knowledge, views the Comcast–Time Warner pact as a blatant antitrust play designed to smother independent web-video innovation in its cradle.

"What Time Warner and Comcast are trying to do here is take the anti-competitive, bundled cable monopoly and map it directly onto the open internet," Sohn says. "By tying web content strictly to expensive, traditional cable subscriptions, they are actively punishing consumers who want alternative choices and trying to make sure no independent online video distributor can ever compete with them. It raises serious antitrust questions. The internet was built on openness, but TV Everywhere is designed to build a tollbooth on every highway."

Sohn points out that if cable providers succeed in forcing all major networks behind subscription login walls, the blossoming ecosystem of web video platforms—from Roku boxes to standalone web portals—could be starved of content before they ever reach critical mass.

For now, the battle lines are drawn. On one side sits Hulu, pushing the web toward an ad-supported, ala-carte future. On the other sit the telecom and media titans, clutching their $40-billion-a-year cable-subscription engine and insisting that the web must adapt to cable, not the other way around.

As those 5,000 test users in the pilot program log into their accounts this week to watch TNT, they aren't just streaming television. They are testing whether the open web can be tamed, packaged, and billed at $80 a month. 

***

*(MIKE MONTGOMERY covers digital media and telecommunications policy for WIRED.)*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news report exploring how traditional cable providers planned to combat cord-cutting in the late 2000s. Focus on Comcast and Time Warner introducing broadband authentication, contrasting the industry's subscription defense against net neutrality and competition concerns raised by consumer advocates.
counterfactuals.output:
**Behind the Wall: Cable Giants Launch ‘TV Everywhere’ Strategy to Head Off Cord-Cutters**

**NEW YORK** — As high-speed internet access expands across American households, the nation’s largest cable providers are moving aggressively to defend their core business against a quiet but growing threat: the web. 

Facing early signs of "cord-cutting"—the emerging trend of consumers dropping expensive set-top boxes in favor of free or cheap online video—industry titans Comcast Corp. and Time Warner Cable are rolling out a new technical architecture designed to keep prime-time television tethered to the traditional cable bundle.

The strategy, championed by Time Warner CEO Jeff Bewkes and Comcast CEO Brian Roberts, is built around a system known as "broadband authentication." Internally dubbed "TV Everywhere," the initiative allows cable subscribers to stream popular cable and broadcast network shows on their computers at no extra cost. 

There is, however, a catch: to watch, viewers must prove they already pay for a traditional, monthly cable television subscription by logging in with their account credentials. Anyone without a cable package is locked out.

### Protecting the Pay-TV Bundle

For the cable industry, broadband authentication is a vital line of defense. Throughout the 2000s, the cable business model thrived on a "dual-revenue stream"—collecting both monthly subscriber fees and local advertising revenues. But the rapid rise of platforms like Hulu, YouTube, and Netflix’s fledgling streaming service has threatened to upend that setup, leading a growing number of cash-strapped consumers to consider surviving on internet video alone.

By launching TV Everywhere, Comcast and Time Warner hope to transform the internet from a competitive threat into a value-added feature of the legacy cable subscription.

"Our goal is to give consumers the content they love on any screen they choose," Comcast executives stated during a recent media briefing, framing the move as a major victory for consumer convenience. "If you pay for video content in the living room, you should be able to take it with you to your laptop."

Under the initiative, trials are currently underway featuring networks from Time Warner’s TNT and TBS to Comcast-aligned channels. If successful, the providers plan to scale authentication across nearly every major cable channel, effectively creating a digital fence around premium television content on the web.

### Consumer Advocates Sound the Alarm

While cable executives view authentication as a logical extension of their distribution rights, consumer advocates, public interest groups, and digital rights organizations view the strategy with deep suspicion. 

Advocacy groups like Free Press and Public Knowledge argue that broadband authentication is an anti-competitive tactic designed to choke off nascent online rivals before they can mature. By tying access to web content directly to a high-margin cable package—which often costs consumers upward of $80 to $100 a month—providers are effectively preventing a true a la carte online video market from developing.

"This isn’t about enhancing the consumer experience; it’s about protecting a legacy monopoly model," said Gigi Sohn, president and co-founder of Public Knowledge. "Instead of competing on the open internet, the cable industry is trying to wall off web content and force consumers to keep paying for 200 channels they don't watch just to get the three shows they do."

Critics point out a fundamental conflict of interest: the very companies that control traditional television delivery also control the broadband pipes delivering internet to American homes. 

### Net Neutrality and Competition Concerns

The push for broadband authentication has also dragged the initiative straight into the escalating national debate over Net Neutrality. 

Consumer advocates worry that internet service providers (ISPs) like Comcast and Time Warner will use their market dominance as broadband gatekeepers to give preferential treatment to their own authenticated services, while slowing down or penalizing independent streaming platforms. 

There are growing concerns that cable ISPs could eventually exempt their own authenticated online video streams from broadband data caps, while applying strict caps to competing services like Netflix. Critics contend such practices would violate the core tenets of an open internet, which dictate that all data traffic should be treated equally regardless of its source or owner.

"If an ISP can use its control over the broadband wire to dictate which business models succeed online, the open web as an engine of innovation is in serious jeopardy," warned S. Derek Turner, research director at Free Press. 

### The Battle for the Living Room

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is monitoring the developments closely, as regulators weigh new rules to enforce open internet principles and ensure fair competition in the rapidly converging telecom and media markets.

For now, the battle lines are drawn. The cable industry is betting billions that consumers will value the convenience of authenticated streaming enough to maintain their monthly subscriptions. Consumer groups, meanwhile, are appealing to regulators to prevent the open web from being carved up into proprietary, gated communities.

As more households upgrade to high-speed connections, the outcome of this clash will determine not just how Americans watch television, but whether the internet remains an open marketplace or becomes an extension of the legacy cable box.

**Cable’s Empire Strikes Back: ‘TV Everywhere’ Wants to Keep You Tethered**

**NEW YORK — 06.24.09 —** For the past two years, the cable industry has watched nervously as millions of viewers migrated toward the frictionless, free-for-all ecosystem of Hulu, YouTube, and digital downloads. The dream of the “cord-cutter”—ditching the $100-a-month cable bill in favor of a web browser and an Ethernet cord—suddenly seemed less like a geek fantasy and more like an impending reality. 

Today, the media giants officially launched their counter-offensive.

Dubbed "TV Everywhere," the ambitious industry-wide initiative promises to bring live television and deep on-demand catalogs straight to your laptop, smartphone, and desktop computer. The catch? You can only watch if you already pay for traditional cable.

Spearheaded by Time Warner CEO Jeff Bewkes and Comcast chief Brian Roberts, TV Everywhere is designed to bridge the gap between old-fashioned living room set-top boxes and the modern, browser-based web. Under the new system, cable subscribers will use a single sign-on—an authentication process the industry calls "pass-through"—to unlock ad-supported cable programming on network websites and mobile apps.

Beginning this week, Comcast is rolling out a trial dubbed "Fancast XFINITY" to roughly 5,000 subscribers, offering content from TNT, TBS, and HBO. Time Warner and Verizon FiOS are expected to follow with their own implementations by the end of the summer.

"If you pay for content, you should be able to get it on any screen you choose," Bewkes said during a press briefing announcing the initiative. "The web isn't the enemy of television—it's just another wire."

To the casual observer, it sounds like a win for consumers who want to stream *Mad Men* or live sports on their MacBooks while traveling. But under the hood, TV Everywhere is a defensive fortress built to protect the multi-billion-dollar carriage fees that keep media conglomerates afloat. 

By locking streaming video behind a cable subscription paywall, the networks hope to undercut the momentum of sites like Hulu, which currently streams network hits for free, funded solely by digital ads. Insiders suggest that as contracts expire over the next 18 months, major networks will begin pulling their newest episodes off free sites and hiding them behind the TV Everywhere gate.

Technologically, the rollout is still a bit of a Frankenstein’s monster. Early demos rely heavily on Adobe Flash and Microsoft Silverlight plugins, and the sign-in process requires users to navigate a maze of cable provider login portals. Furthermore, rights management remains a logistical nightmare: sports leagues, movie studios, and local affiliates are all scrambling to renegotiate digital streaming rights, meaning the selection at launch will feel noticeably patchy compared to a full cable guide.

There is also the question of mobile. While the iPhone 3GS and palm Pre have proven that handheld video playback is finally viable, cellular networks are already choking on data. Whether AT&T and Verizon can handle millions of users streaming high-definition television over 3G networks remains an open, expensive question.

Early reactions from the web community are mixed. Tech-savvy consumers who have spent the last few years trying to escape the rigid bundle of cable television view the initiative as a backward step—an attempt to force 1990s business models onto the open web. 

Yet, for the vast majority of Americans who aren't ready to unplug their set-top boxes just yet, TV Everywhere offers a compelling compromise: the convenience of web video without having to wait for torrents to download or DVDs to arrive in the mail from Netflix.

The cable industry is betting heavily that convenience will win out over digital freedom. Whether web users will tolerate logging in to watch the shows they used to get for free remains to be seen. But one thing is clear: the battle for the future of the living room has officially moved to the browser.

# The End of the Free Lunch: Why Big Cable Is Building a Paywall Around the Web

**For years, the entertainment industry let us watch prime-time TV online for free. Now, Time Warner CEO Jeff Bewkes and his media brethren are locking down the browser—and demanding your cable login.**

**By Jason Tanz** | *10.27.2009 | 12:00 PM*

For the past two years, watching television on the internet has felt like a victimless crime—or better yet, a utopian free-for-all. 

Did you miss last night’s episode of *30 Rock*? No problem: boot up Hulu, ignore a couple of thirty-second Lexus ads, and stream it in glorious 720p. Want to catch up on *Mad Men*? Just hit up AMC’s website or fire up BitTorrent. The web, it seemed, had finally liberated television from the physical constraints of the set-top box. We were all cord-cutters in training, happily surfing on a wave of venture-backed, ad-supported, zero-cost content.

Enjoy it while it lasts. The free lunch is officially over.

Over the past few months, a cabal of the country’s biggest media executives—led by Comcast’s Brian Roberts and Time Warner CEO Jeff Bewkes—has been quietly laying the pipe for a massive web-wide lockdown. They call it "TV Everywhere," though a more accurate name might be "TV Only If You Pay The Cable Company First."

The premise is simple, if frustratingly regressive: If you want to stream full episodes of network and cable TV on your laptop, iPhone, or web browser, you will soon have to log in using the credentials of your existing, paid cable or satellite subscription. No subscription? No stream. 

Welcome to the age of authenticated video.

### The $100 Billion Panic

To understand why traditional media is suddenly rushing to build a paywall around the open web, you only have to look at the cratering balance sheets of 2009. The Great Recession has decimated the digital ad market. The promise that online banner ads and pre-roll clips could offset the decline of traditional broadcast advertising has evaporated into thin air. 

At the center of this pivot is Jeff Bewkes, the polished, silver-haired chief executive of Time Warner. Unlike some of his old-school media peers who viewed the internet merely as a haven for piracy and cat videos, Bewkes saw the web clearly—and he realized it was destroying his business model.

"The idea that high-quality, expensive television programming should be free on the internet just because it's delivered digitally is fundamentally broken," Bewkes tells *WIRED* from his Manhattan office. "It’s a fantasy. If you give away the content for free online, you undermine the very ecosystem that pays to produce the content in the first place."

That ecosystem is the holy grail of media finance: the "dual-revenue stream." For decades, cable networks like HBO, TNT, and ESPN have made money twice—first from local cable operators who pay a monthly per-subscriber fee, and second from traditional advertisers. Free streaming sites like Hulu, Bewkes argues, stripped away the subscriber fee, leaving networks relying solely on fraction-of-a-penny digital ads.

"We spent 30 years building a system where consumers pay a small, bundled monthly price for hundreds of channels of incredible quality," Bewkes says. "You can’t just replace that with a few banner ads on a browser and expect *Game of Thrones* or *The Pacific* to get made. Free is not a business model. It's a race to the bottom."

### The "TV Everywhere" Solution

Enter TV Everywhere. Jointly championed by Time Warner and Comcast, the system acts as a digital velvet rope. 

Here’s how it works: You head to TNT.tv or HBO.com to watch the latest episode of *The Closer*. Before the video player loads, a pop-up window asks you to select your television provider—say, Comcast Xfinity or Time Warner Cable. You enter your cable account username and password. The system verifies that you pay for cable in the real world, and *voilà*: the stream begins.

If you don't have cable? You get a trailer, a 90-second clip, and a link to buy a cable package.

To the technorati, this feels like a desperate, backward-looking move—an attempt by legacy gatekeepers to drag the frictionless, open web back into the era of closed networks and monthly bills. It’s the digital equivalent of requiring a physical ticket stub just to enter a discussion about a movie.

Critics point out that the user experience of these early TV Everywhere portals is, to put it politely, a trainwreck. Flash-player glitches, forgotten passwords, and clunky identity verification systems threaten to turn legal viewing into a nightmare, practically begging users to flee back to Pirate Bay.

But Bewkes remains unfazed by the tech world’s groans. To him, the digital realm isn't a magical new frontier where the laws of economics are suspended; it’s just another pipe.

"Consumers don't expect their electricity to be free just because it comes out of a different wall socket," Bewkes snaps. "Why should television be any different? What we are saying with TV Everywhere is: You’ve paid for this content. You own the right to watch it. We want to give it to you on your PC, on your mobile device, anywhere you go—but you still have to pay for the content."

### Hulu in the Crosshairs

The biggest casualty in this war over online video might be Hulu itself. Launched in 2007 as a joint venture between NBC Universal and News Corp (and later Disney), Hulu was hailed as the slick, consumer-friendly savior of network television. 

But behind the scenes, media executives are quietly panicking about Hulu's success. By offering current-season episodes for free the morning after they air, Hulu gave young, internet-savvy viewers—the exact demographic cable companies are terrified of losing—a reason to never sign up for cable in the first place.

Rumors are already circulating through Silicon Valley and Midtown Manhattan that Hulu will soon be forced to implement its own subscription tier (provisionally dubbed "Hulu Plus") or adopt the TV Everywhere authentication model for its most popular shows.

"Hulu was a great experiment in aggregation," says James McQuivey, a principal analyst at Forrester Research. "But it proved that ad-supported free video can’t support the budget of prime-time television. Cable companies hold all the leverage. They pay the affiliate fees. If Comcast and Time Warner tell the networks, 'Lock down your web video or we stop paying you,' the networks will lock it down overnight."

### The Battle for the Living Room

The irony of the TV Everywhere push is that it comes just as the hardware for web-to-TV streaming is finally getting good. Roku’s tiny $99 streaming box is gaining traction, Apple is rumored to be revamping its sluggish Apple TV, and video game consoles like the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 are rapidly morphing into living-room media hubs.

The cable industry knows that if high-definition streams remain free on the web, consumers will plug an HDMI cable into their laptops, bypass the cable box entirely, and cut the cord forever. By locking web video behind a cable login, Bewkes and his allies aren't just protecting their current revenue—they are attempting to colonize the future of television before Silicon Valley can claim it.

Will consumers accept the new paywalls? Or will a generation raised on Napster, YouTube, and free Hulu simply tune out?

Jeff Bewkes is betting $100 billion that when faced with the choice between paying for premium TV or watching amateur clip shows on YouTube, viewers will reach for their wallets.

"People value great storytelling," Bewkes says, leaning back in his chair. "They'll pay for it on a cathode-ray tube, they'll pay for it on a plasma screen, and they'll pay for it on a laptop screen. The device changes. The value of the content doesn't."

The era of the wild-west web video is officially ending. The cable guy has arrived on the internet—and he’s bringing the bill.
